standard.title: Language presents characters and settings
standard.description: discuss the characters and settings of a range of texts and identify how language is used to present these features in different ways
standard.prior_knowledge: Students discuss plot, character and setting as features of stories (AC9E1LE03). They have not yet examined how specific language choices present characters and settings differently across texts.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students can identify how language is used to present characters and settings in different ways across a range of texts.

nodes.label: Language that describes character
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify language — specific nouns and adjectives — used to describe a character's appearance and personality, and explain what impression that language creates.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify two language features — at least one noun and one adjective — used to describe a character and explain the impression each creates.
nodes.typical_width: Identify and compare the language used to describe characters across multiple texts, noticing how different word choices create different impressions of similar character types.
wider: Compare how a hero and a villain in the same text are described using contrasting language choices, and discuss how the author uses language to position the reader
Examine how a character is described at the start vs the end of a narrative and identify how language reflects character change
nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Language comparison across contrasting characters (hero/villain, strong/weak) is rich and generative. Students can explore how word choice positions readers to sympathise or distrust — a genuinely meaningful direction within Year 2.
success_criteria: Student can identify specific language used to describe a character and explain the impression it creates.
Student can name at least one noun and one adjective from the character description and explain how each contributes.

nodes.label: Language that creates a sense of place
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify language used to create a sense of place in a text — specific nouns, adjectives and verbs — and explain how they establish the setting.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify two language features used to describe a setting and explain what they contribute to the sense of place.
nodes.typical_width: Identify and discuss setting language across multiple texts — urban, natural, fantastical, familiar — comparing how language features create different atmospheric effects.
wider: Compare how two authors describe the same type of setting (e.g. a forest, a beach) using different language choices, and discuss the different effects
Identify language that creates a sense of Australian place — including references to specific landscapes, flora and fauna — and compare with settings from world literature
success_criteria: Student can identify specific language used to describe a setting and explain what it contributes to the sense of place.
Student can compare language features across at least two settings from different texts.

nodes.label: Different presentations of the same feature
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify that different authors use different language to present similar characters or settings, and discuss the different effects produced.
nodes.minimum_width: Compare two texts with a similar character type or setting and name one language difference that creates a different presentation.
nodes.typical_width: Discuss how a range of texts present similar features differently — through vocabulary, tone, description density — and explain how different language choices produce different effects on the reader.
wider: Compare presentations of a familiar character archetype (e.g. the wise elder, the brave child) across texts from different cultural contexts and discuss how cultural context shapes the language
Identify how the same setting is presented differently in a narrative vs an information text and discuss what this reveals about purpose and language

response_modes.reason: This node integrates character-language and setting-language knowledge across texts. Holding multiple texts in view simultaneously and comparing specific language choices is the coordination demand.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Cross-cultural character comparisons are genuinely rich — they show students that literary conventions are not universal and that language choices reflect cultural values. This is meaningful enrichment within the Year 2 band.
success_criteria: Student can name a language difference between two texts presenting similar features and explain the different effect each creates.
Student can discuss why different authors might choose different language to present similar characters or settings.
